title: Fracture
path: First Aid Management of Patients with Medical and Surgical Emergencies

headings.title: Definition and Types of Fractures
headings.content: A fracture is defined as a disruption or break in the continuity of the bone structure, often resulting from mechanical forces that exceed the bone's inherent tensile or compressive strength. Understanding the various classifications of fractures is essential for nursing students in Nigeria, as treatment and management plans depend heavily on the type of bone injury sustained. Fractures are broadly categorized into closed (simple) and open (compound) fractures. A closed fracture occurs when the skin integrity remains intact over the fracture site, minimizing the immediate risk of external contamination. Conversely, an open fracture involves a break in the skin and underlying soft tissues, exposing the bone directly to the external environment and significantly elevating the risk of osteomyelitis and serious infections. Furthermore, fractures can be classified based on the configuration of the break, such as transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, greenstick, and impacted fractures. Transverse fractures run straight across the bone shaft, whereas oblique fractures occur at an angle. Spiral fractures twist around the bone shaft, often suggestive of rotational trauma or potential non-accidental injury. Comminuted fractures feature multiple bone fragments, greenstick fractures are incomplete breaks commonly seen in children due to their pliable bones, and impacted fractures occur when bone fragments are driven into each other. Recognizing these distinct types enables nurses to anticipate clinical interventions, comprehend radiological reports, and provide targeted patient education throughout the recovery trajectory.

headings.title: Pathophysiology and Underlying Concepts
headings.content: The pathophysiology of bone fracture healing is a dynamic, highly orchestrated physiological process that restores structural and functional integrity to the injured bone. This complex biological response generally progresses through three overlapping stages: the inflammatory phase, the reparative phase, and the remodeling phase. Immediately following a fracture, blood vessels rupture, causing local hemorrhage and the formation of a fracture hematoma within the injury site. During the inflammatory phase, lasting approximately the first 24 to 72 hours, neutrophils and macrophages infiltrate the area to phagocytize debris and necrotic tissue, releasing cytokines that trigger angiogenesis and cellular proliferation. Following inflammation, the reparative phase begins, characterized by the development of a fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus. Fibroblasts and osteoblasts migrate into the hematoma, secreting collagen and forming a bridge of soft tissue across the fracture ends. Over the subsequent weeks, osteoblasts deposit mineralized bone matrix, transforming the soft callus into a hard, bony callus visible on radiographs. The final stage, bone remodeling, can take months to years. During this prolonged period, osteoclasts resorb excess bony callus while osteoblasts lay down new compact bone along lines of mechanical stress, ultimately restoring the bone to its original shape, strength, and structural configuration.

headings.title: Causes and Risk Factors
headings.content: Fractures occur when physical forces exerted on the skeletal system surpass the load-bearing capacity of the bone tissue. Determining the underlying causes and identifying specific risk factors are critical components of comprehensive nursing assessment and preventative healthcare planning. The primary causes of fractures can be categorized into acute traumatic events, fatigue or stress injuries, and pathological conditions. Traumatic fractures are typically the result of high-energy mechanisms such as motor vehicle accidents, falls from a height, industrial machinery mishaps, or physical assaults, which are frequently encountered in emergency settings across Nigeria. Stress fractures, on the other hand, arise from repetitive, cumulative microtrauma exceeding the bone's ability to repair itself, commonly seen in athletes or individuals initiating intense physical conditioning. Pathological fractures occur spontaneously or with minimal trauma in bones already weakened by an underlying disease process. Common underlying pathologies include osteoporosis, primary or metastatic bone malignancies, Paget's disease, and certain endocrine or nutritional disorders like osteomalacia. Risk factors that heighten vulnerability to fractures include advanced age, postmenopausal status due to estrogen depletion, sedentary lifestyle, inadequate dietary calcium and Vitamin D intake, tobacco use, chronic corticosteroid therapy, and visual or neurological impairments that increase fall risks. By screening patients for these risk factors, nurses can implement targeted fall prevention strategies and advocate for bone health education.

headings.title: Clinical Manifestations and Assessment
headings.content: Performing a prompt and thorough clinical assessment is vital for detecting fractures, evaluating the extent of tissue damage, and preventing secondary neurovascular complications. Nurses must be adept at recognizing both subjective symptoms and objective clinical manifestations of bone injury. Classical signs and symptoms of a fracture include localized pain or tenderness at the site of injury, immediate loss of functional capacity, obvious anatomical deformity, swelling resulting from edema and hemorrhage, bruising or ecchymosis, muscle spasms, and crepitus—a grating sensation caused by bone fragments rubbing together. When assessing an injured extremity, the nurse must systematically evaluate the neurovascular status using the crucial '6 Ps' mnemonic: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paresthesia, Paralysis, and Poikilothermia (coolness of the extremity). Any deficit in pulse quality, capillary refill, sensory perception, or motor movement points toward compromised blood flow or nerve compression, demanding immediate medical notification. Diagnostic confirmation is primarily achieved through standard plain radiography (X-rays) taken from multiple views to visualize the exact fracture line and displacement. In more complex scenarios involving joint involvement or subtle stress fractures, advanced imaging modalities such as computed tomography (CT) scans or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may be utilized to formulate an effective therapeutic strategy.

headings.title: Emergency First Aid Management
headings.content: Immediate emergency first aid management at the scene of a fracture is crucial to prevent further injury to surrounding soft tissues, blood vessels, and nerves. The primary golden rule of emergency fracture care is to immobilize the body part before moving or transporting the patient. Nurses and first responders must assess the scene for safety hazards, ensure a patent airway, check breathing and circulation, and control any external bleeding using direct pressure on the wound while avoiding direct manipulation of protruding bone ends. If an open fracture is present, the exposed bone should be covered with a sterile, moist dressing to minimize bacterial contamination, but no attempt should be made to push the bone back into the tissue. Splinting is the cornerstone of emergency management; it immobilizes the joints above and below the fracture site to decrease pain, reduce muscle spasms, prevent sharp bone fragments from lacerating adjacent neurovascular structures, and limit fat embolism formation. Various materials can be used for splinting, including rigid boards, air splints, pillows, or even utilizing an uninjured limb as a makeshift splint for lower extremities. Following application, the nurse or responder must continuously re-check distal neurovascular status—including pulses, capillary refill, and sensation—to ensure that the splint or bandage is not constrictive. Prompt transfer to a healthcare facility is then arranged for definitive orthopedic diagnosis and intervention.

headings.title: Medical and Surgical Treatment Interventions
headings.content: Medical and surgical interventions for fractures aim to achieve anatomical reduction, stable fixation, and early functional restoration. Reduction refers to the restoration of bone fragments to their correct alignment and length. This can be accomplished through closed reduction, a non-surgical manual realignment procedure performed under local or general anesthesia, followed by the application of immobilization devices such as plaster or fiberglass casts, traction, or functional braces. Traction utilizes a pulling force to realign fractured bones and can be skin traction (Buck's traction) or skeletal traction, where pins or wires are surgically inserted directly into the bone. When closed methods are insufficient to maintain alignment, or when dealing with complex, unstable, or open fractures, surgical intervention becomes necessary. Open reduction internal fixation (ORIF) involves a surgical incision to directly visualize the fracture site, realign the bone fragments, and secure them using internal hardware such as metal plates, screws, intramedullary nails, or pins. Alternatively, external fixation involves placing percutaneous pins through the skin and bone above and below the fracture, connecting them to an external metal frame outside the limb. External fixation is frequently used for severe open fractures with extensive soft tissue damage, allowing wound access while maintaining bone stability. Nursing management during these interventions involves meticulous pin site care, monitoring for signs of infection, managing pain, and assisting with early mobilization protocols.

headings.title: Potential Complications
headings.content: Fractures can precipitate a variety of localized and systemic complications that require vigilant nursing monitoring and prompt multidisciplinary intervention. Early identification of these complications is critical for preventing permanent disability or life-threatening outcomes. One of the most severe local complications is Compartment Syndrome, a condition where increased pressure within a confined muscle compartment restricts blood flow, leading to severe, unrelenting pain that is unrelieved by opioids, diminished pulses, and potential tissue necrosis. Fasciotomy is often required if compartment pressure remains elevated. Another significant local risk is osteomyelitis, a severe bone infection commonly associated with open fractures or surgical fixation, which requires prolonged antibiotic therapy. Fat embolism syndrome (FES) is a serious systemic complication that predominantly occurs following fractures of long bones, such as the femur, when fat globules enter the bloodstream and occlude small vessels in the lungs and brain. Classic clinical triads of FES include hypoxemia, neurological abnormalities (such as confusion or restlessness), and a distinct petechial rash across the chest and neck. Other potential complications include deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and pulmonary embolism (PE) resulting from venous stasis during immobilization, delayed union or nonunion where the bone fails to heal properly, and avascular necrosis (AVN) due to compromised blood supply to the bone head, particularly in femoral neck fractures. Nurses must maintain high clinical suspicion and perform frequent systematic assessments to catch these complications early.

headings.title: Nursing Care and Rehabilitation
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care and rehabilitation are essential for helping patients recover optimal physical function, regain independence, and prevent long-term disability following a fracture. The nursing plan of care encompasses meticulous cast and traction maintenance, pain management, nutritional support, prevention of immobility-related complications, and coordination with physical and occupational therapists. When caring for a patient in a plaster cast, nurses must handle the wet cast with the palms of their hands to prevent indentation points that can cause pressure ulcers underneath, keep the limb elevated to minimize edema, and routinely assess neurovascular status and skin integrity around the cast edges. For patients undergoing traction, weights must hang freely without touching the floor or bed frame, and ropes must remain unobstructed in their pulleys. Nurses should encourage a balanced, nutrient-dense diet high in protein, calcium, Vitamin C, and Vitamin D to support bone healing and tissue regeneration. To combat the hazards of immobility, nurses implement preventative measures such as encouraging deep breathing exercises, early ambulation or range-of-motion exercises, hydration to prevent urinary tract infections, and repositioning every two hours. Rehabilitation begins early in the recovery process, with physical therapists guiding progressive weight-bearing exercises and muscle-strengthening routines tailored to the patient's specific fracture type and fixation method. Finally, discharge education must cover warning signs of complications, safe use of assistive devices like crutches or walkers, and the importance of follow-up appointments.
